messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: autodiff distributions
parts:
Hi folks,

I checked in a new file stan/prob/ag_distributions.hpp, which
specializes normal_log() to do the autodiff gradient calculations more
efficiently. Whereas before calling normal_log() would do autodiff
through all of the calculations needed to compute the normal log
probability, the new specialized version computes the gradients
analytically, which turns out to be a good amount faster, like a
factor of 2 over the previous version on the rats example. This is
comparable to the speed I get when doing "by hand" code generation
using adjoint variables, and within a factor of two of the speed I get
with more highly tuned handwritten gradient code. All of which seems
to suggest that this is something that we should be doing for other
distributions too.

I've also checked in a version of rats.cpp* that illustrates how to
use the new ag_distributions implementation. You can test the speed
change on your own machine by commenting out "#include
<stan/prob/ag_distributions.hpp>".

We should probably think harder about what the right way to do these
implementations is in general—I just threw something together quickly
as a proof of concept.

Matt

*This model expresses things in terms of precisions instead of
deviations, but the differences should be minimal.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] autodiff distributions
parts:
That's great. I figured we'd start doing these
as we needed them. I'm very pleased it's so much
faster.

We should eventually do all the distributions. With
design as it stands, we should be able to drop
in optimizations like this as we go in a way that's
backward compatible. We can keep going with
structured subroutines for reusable parts of models.
I've been planning out the within-Stan subroutine
language, but that won't make things go faster.

The matrix ops could use the same treatment -- many
of them have easy analytical derivatives. Including
Ben's covariance encoding. It's just an awful lot of code
and doc to deal with. Daniel and I did just get error
handling sorted and this is another argument for doing
things with the kind of helper functions he set up.

The next step is to get rid of constant terms from
the calc. We can do that with template overrides.
For example, what we have now is:

template <typename T_y, typename T_loc, typename T_scale>
calculated_type
normal_log(T_y y, T_loc mu, T_scale sigma);

What we eventually need is eight template overrides based on
whether T_y, T_loc, T_scale are stan::agrad::var
or double instances. Then for each instance, drop all
the terms that just involve double values as they'll be
in the constant normalizer. For instance,
we can use the following for non-hierarchical regression
priors:

template <>
var
normal_log(var y, double mu, double sigma) {
... doesn't involve log(sigma) term ...
}

Then we can drop any terms in the sum that only have
double args as they're just constant normalizing terms.

Then we can do the same thing with multiple samples,
adding another 8 versions with std::vector<T_y>
as the first arg in the general case.
For the normal, that saves a whole lot of log calcs
if the scale is stan::agrad::var.

For consistency, the code should go in namespace
stan::agrad and in file stan/agrad/distributions.hpp. This
will require more includes, though I want to
add some higher-level includes like all the other
packages use.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] autodiff distributions
parts:
The thing about the namespacing is that it affects how things get
overloaded. Putting the specialization in stan::agrad won't actually
overload stan::prob::normal_log(). So things get ambiguous unless you
explicitly say stan::agrad::normal_log(), which won't work for the
nonspecialized versions.

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] autodiff distributions
parts:
On 11/14/11 9:19 AM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> The thing about the namespacing is that it affects how things get
> overloaded. Putting the specialization in stan::agrad won't actually
> overload stan::prob::normal_log(). So things get ambiguous unless you
> explicitly say stan::agrad::normal_log(), which won't work for the
> nonspecialized versions.

Ah, of course -- thanks for pointing that out. Template
overriding isn't the same as simple function overloading.

Because the base function should go in stan::prob, that
seems to give us two choices: (a) override the templates
in stan::prob, or (b) overload the functions in stan::agrad.
We've followed path (b) with the basic functions out
of necessity -- some of them were in the std lib.

Is there a reason to prefer one over the other?

We'll still be able to keep the modules independent
at the include level, so that someone could include
prob without including agrad.

Parts of Eigen where you specify traits for numericals
(as we do for auto-dif), require you to do it in their
namespace.

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] autodiff distributions
parts:
As I see it:

Pros to putting them in stan::prob
* There aren't separate versions of the functions floating around in
two namespaces. Overloading the functions in stan::agrad makes it
possible for people to still call stan::prob::normal_log<var, var,
var>(), possibly by accident if things are included in the wrong order
(actually, I don't know how these ambiguities are resolved).
* There's no need to do the overloading in stan::agrad. I guess this
wouldn't be so bad—we can just have something like
template<...>
inline boost::promote_args<...> normal_log(...) {
return stan::prob::normal_log(...);
}
but it's still one more thing that needs doing.

Pros to putting them in stan::agrad
* Keeps all the autodiff stuff out of stan::prob.
* It's still possible to call stan::prob::normal_log() with vars if
you really really want to, although I'm not sure why you would
(assuming that we don't mess up the specialized implementations).

I'm inclined to say we should put them in a separate include file and
in stan::prob, since it eliminates some ambiguity and involves less
coding. But I could certainly be convinced otherwise if people feel
differently.

Matt
